refuted.claim: "the 1402 unconditionally transfers exactly 80 characters from the read buffer" (findings summary and the Figure-61 table row "Transfer 80 characters from read buffer to core storage" presented as unconditional).
refuted.why: A22-0526-3 'Read a Card' says both things: the instruction 'causes the transfer of 80 characters from the card-read buffer to core storage', but then 'The operation is stopped by the first group-mark - word-mark sensed in core storage.' and under Word Marks: 'A group-mark-word-mark must appear in the core-storage position to the immediate right of the data record... If the [group-mark-word-mark] is incorrectly positioned, the wrong-length record channel status indicator will turn on.' 80 is the buffer size, not an unconditional store count. SimH implements exactly this: i7010_chan.c terminates the record when 'M[caddr[chan]] == (WM|077)' (group mark + word mark) and sets IO_CHS_WRL. An emulator that always writes 80 characters will silently diverge on every normal (d='R') card read.
refuted.correction: A 1402 Read a Card moves UP TO 80 characters from the read buffer into core starting at the B-address, terminating on the first group-mark-word-mark in core storage; the wrong-length-record I/O channel status indicator is set if the GMWM is not exactly one position past the 80th character. The unconditional-80 behaviour only happens with the d-character that suppresses the GMWM test (see next item).
refuted.source: A22-0526-3 IBM 1410 Principles of Operation, 'Read a Card', pp. 61-62 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf ; SimH I7000/i7010_chan.c (record-end test on WM|077) - https://github.com/simh/simh/blob/master/I7000/i7010_chan.c

refuted.claim: "There is no card-reader '$' variant in the instruction list, so an emulator should decode the 1402 read on op code + x-control field alone and ignore the d-character (accept both '$' and 'R')." And the interpretive claim that "The '$' is IBM re-using one template across tape and card."
refuted.why: On the 1410 the d-character of an I/O instruction is decoded by the CPU/channel, not by the device, and it selects the record-termination rule. A22-0526-3 p.86 defines '$' as 'read to IRG or end of core', for which 'Group-mark-word-marks in core storage have no effect'; 'R' is the variant that stops on a GMWM. SimH encodes exactly that split device-independently: i7010_cpu.c OP_RD maps CHR_R -> (IO_RDS<<8) and CHR_DOL ('$') -> (IO_RDS<<8)|0100, and i7010_chan.c chan_cmd() turns that 0100 bit into CHAN_NOREC, which suppresses the group-mark-word-mark record-end test for every device including the card reader. Ignoring d would break the documented boot: after COMPUTER RESET on a cleared machine there is no group-mark-word-mark anywhere, so an 'R' read has no terminator and sets wrong-length-record; '$' is precisely the modifier that says 'ignore GMWM, fill to end of record/core'. The Monitor's use of '$' on the card path is therefore deliberate, not template sloppiness.
refuted.correction: Keep the d-character load-bearing on a 1402 read: 'R' = stop on group-mark-word-mark in core (set WLR if misplaced); '$' = ignore group-mark-word-marks and take the whole 80-character buffer. Decode d at channel level, before device dispatch.
refuted.source: A22-0526-3, 'Read or Write Tape' (d-character R vs $), p. 86 and 'Read a Card', p. 62 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf ; SimH I7000/i7010_cpu.c case OP_RD (CHR_DOL -> |0100) and I7000/i7010_chan.c chan_cmd() ('if (dcmd & 0100) /* Mod $ or X */ cmd[chan] |= CHAN_NOREC;') - https://github.com/simh/simh/tree/master/I7000

refuted.claim: "r = R for channel 1, X for channel 2, 3 for channel 3, 1 for channel 4" and "c = channel symbol (% / lozenge / ? / !)" presented as 1410 facts (fact 8 and the two tables).
refuted.why: This is 1410-vs-7010 conflation. C28-0351-5 is a joint 1410/7010 Operating System manual, so its Table II lists all four channels; but A22-0526-3 (the 1410 machine manual) documents only two I/O channels. 'Branch if I/O Channel Status Indicator On' says: 'All use the R op code for channel 1 or the X op code for channel 2' - there is no channel-3 or channel-4 branch op code on a 1410. Likewise the x-control hundreds position lists exactly four symbols on the 1410: '%' channel 1 non-overlap, '@' channel 1 overlap, lozenge channel 2 non-overlap, '*' channel 2 overlap. SimH's i7010_cpu.c OP_RD decoder does accept '?'/'!' (ch 3/4) and '$'/'=' (ch 3/4 overlap), but that is the 7010 machine, which i7010 also emulates.
refuted.correction: On a 1410, only R (channel 1) and X (channel 2) exist as status-branch op codes, and only % / @ / lozenge / * are valid in the x1 position. The '?' and '!' channel symbols and the '3' and '1' status-branch op codes are 7010-only; a 1410 emulator should never reach them (and arguably should raise an instruction check).
refuted.source: A22-0526-3, 'Branch if I/O Channel Status Indicator On', p. 37 and 'Overlap Versus Non-Overlap Operations' (x1 symbol table), p. 92 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf ; C28-0351-5 Table II, p. 8 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/C28-0351-5_1410_operGuide.pdf

refuted.claim: "every I/O instruction sets an interlock that stops the machine if it is still on when the next I/O instruction is read out" (fact 9 and the summary), stated without channel qualification.
refuted.why: The p.42 summary paragraph does omit the qualifier, but the normative statement in the instruction description does not: 'To avoid stopping the system, one of these instructions must be given between two i/o instructions ON THE SAME CHANNEL... if it is still on when the next i/o instruction is read out ON THE SAME CHANNEL, the system stops.' An emulator that models one global interlock will wrongly halt on legitimate interleaved channel-1 / channel-2 I/O. The same paragraph also enumerates which op codes arm the interlock, which the findings omit.
refuted.correction: The interlock and the six status indicators are per channel. The I/O op codes that arm it are M, L, U, F, 2, K and 4. It is cleared by (1) an X- or R(I)group-mark instruction given before the next I/O instruction on that channel, with no branch required, or (2) any specific X- or R-type status branch that actually branches.
refuted.source: A22-0526-3, 'Branch if I/O Channel Status Indicator On', p. 37 (and the summary at 'Results of Omitting the Status Test', p. 42) - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

refuted.claim: Summary prose: "the operator hand-keys an 11-character I/O instruction into 00001-00011" (an internal inconsistency - the findings' own table gets this right).
refuted.why: A22-0526-3 'Instruction Length Validity' fixes the legal instruction lengths at 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11 and 12 characters, with the I/O form being 'O xxx bbbbb d = 10 positions'. The keyed string is a 10-character I/O instruction at 00001-00010 plus a separate one-character op code (the R/X status branch) at 00011, whose I-address (00012-00016) and d-character (00017) are supplied by the card that has just been read. There is no 11-character I/O instruction.
refuted.correction: 10-character I/O instruction at 00001-00010, plus 1 branch op code at 00011 = 11 keyed instruction positions, 12 characters total counting the initialization status character at 00000.

upgraded.claim: The Bootstrap 1 routine card layout for the 1410 System (findings fact 9, marked 'likely'): cols 1-5 = 00018, col 6 = a group-mark glyph, col 7 = word separator, col 8 onward = 'L xF0 00066 R ...' ending in a J 00138 branch, cols 77-80 = 1410. Confirmed by re-reading C28-0351-5 p. 8 at 400 dpi. Full transcription: cols 1-5 '00018'; col 6 group mark; col 7 word separator; cols 8-17 'L x F 0 0 0 0 6 6 R' (= L, x-control 'xF0', B-address 00066, d 'R'); col 18 word separator; cols 19-25 'y 00035 [group mark]'; col 26 word separator; cols 27-36 'L x F 1 0 0 0 6 6 $'; col 37 word separator; cols 38-44 'y 00035 2'; col 45 word separator; cols 46-52 'y 00059 [group mark]'; col 53 word separator; cols 54-59 'J 00138'; then '[word separator] a m t t t t h 2 [word separator] [group mark]'; cols 77-80 '1410'. Legend on the card: x = % ch1 / lozenge ch2 System Operating File; y = R ch1 / X ch2; a = access mechanism, m = module, tttth2 = geometric record address. Loading in load mode at 00012 puts the word-marked L at 00018 (the branch target the keyed R uses), the status branch at 00028 falling through to 00035, the second read at 00035, a retry-if-busy branch (d '2') at 00045, a status branch at 00052, J 00138 at 00059, and the 8-character disk control field at 00066 followed by a group-mark-word-mark - which is exactly the B-address 00066 both reads carry. Every address is self-consistent, which is why this transcription can be trusted.
upgraded.source: C28-0351-5 IBM 1410/7010 Operating System Operator's Guide, 'Bootstrap 1 routine card for 1410 System', p. 8, read from a 400 dpi render (pdftoppm -r 400 -f 8) - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/C28-0351-5_1410_operGuide.pdf

upgraded.claim: Open question 4 resolved: the glyph in column 6 of the Bootstrap 1 card is the GROUP MARK, not the record mark. The same glyph appears again at the end of the card immediately after the disk control field, where it can only be a group-mark-word-mark (the field terminator that both reads' B-address 00066 implies), and Figure 36 states 'The group mark has all the bits needed to test all of the above six indicators' - the only d-character that clears the I/O interlock without an actual branch.
upgraded.source: C28-0351-5 p. 8 (400 dpi render) and A22-0526-3 Figure 36, p. 37 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

upgraded.claim: C28-0351-5 Table II variable characters, re-read from a 300 dpi render of p. 8: 'Enter ALcde00012$r into location 00000'. 'c' is: % channel 1, lozenge channel 2, ? channel 3, ! channel 4. 'd' is: 1 card reader, B tape. 'e' is: 0 card reader, 0-9 tape. 'r' is: R channel 1, X channel 2, 3 channel 3, 1 channel 4. Installation-standard line: 'A L__ __ __ 0 0 0 1 2 $ __' with the inverted-circumflex word-mark caret printed over the L and over the blank for r, and the note '"A" can have a word mark.' The finder's e = 0 for the card reader is correct (the archive.org OCR interleaves the four lists and drops it).
upgraded.source: C28-0351-5, Table II 'Initialization with Disk System Operating File', p. 8 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/C28-0351-5_1410_operGuide.pdf

upgraded.claim: Autocoder condensed card format (findings table 3) confirmed field by field from a 300 dpi render of C28-0309-1 p. 7, including the column numbers the OCR drops: col 1 word separator (0-5-8 punch); cols 2-6 xxxxx = high-order position of the area into which the data in cols 13-72 is to be loaded; col 7 word separator; cols 8-10 = 0 0 0 (slashed zeros); cols 11-12 xx = number of characters to be loaded from this card; col 13 onward instructions/data; relocation indicators occupy cols 72, 71, 70; cols 73-80 ignored by the Load Program, with the processor putting a sequence number in 73-75 and the identification in 76-80. Notes verbatim as reported.
upgraded.source: C28-0309-1 IBM 1410 Autocoder, Figure 2 'Condensed Card Format', p. 7 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/C28-0309-1_1410_autocoder.pdf

upgraded.claim: Everything checked in the A22-0526-3 opcode/format spot-check held: (1) 'A program reset or computer reset automatically loads 00001 into the iar' (p. 9); (2) NOP op code N, 'L = 1, 2, 3 No Limit', 'can be substituted for the operation code of any instruction to make that instruction ineffective' (p. 24); (3) Branch if I/O Channel Status Indicator On, form op + iiiii + d = 7 positions, T = 4.5(L+1+C), R = ch 1 / X = ch 2 (p. 37); (4) the two interlock-clearing provisions, verbatim (p. 42); (5) load mode input: a single word separator stored as a word mark over the next incoming character, two consecutive separators stored as one separator, record shortened one position either way (p. 41); (6) Read a Card: M or L, x-control %1x, bbbbb, d = R; x3 = 0/1/2 stacker, 9 = transfer buffer with no feed and no stacker select; T = 49.5 + I/O (pp. 61-62); (7) Select Stacker and Feed: op K (ch 1) / 4 (ch 2), d = 0, 1 or 2, T = 13.5 + I/O (p. 62); (8) Punch a Card: M or L, %4x, bbbbb, d = W, x3 must be 0, 4 or 8 (p. 63); (9) Read or Write Tape: M, %Ux3 (even parity) or %Bx3 (odd parity), bbbbb, d = R/W (stop on IRG or GMWM) or $/X (GMWM has no effect, stop on IRG or end of core); $ and X cannot be overlapped (p. 86); (10) x-control field always 3 positions, x1 = % / @ / lozenge / *, max-form I/O instruction = 10 positions (p. 92); (11) control keys are start, stop, program reset (Figure 48) plus computer reset - no Load key; both resets 'reset the program to 00001' (pp. 50-51); (12) ALTER requires a completed DISPLAY of the location first, and 'Any previously displayed word mark must be re-entered into storage' (p. 51).
upgraded.source: A22-0526-3 IBM 1410 Principles of Operation, pp. 9, 11, 24, 37, 41, 42, 50-51, 61-63, 86, 92 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

upgraded.claim: A22-6726 p. 58 LOAD KEY verified verbatim, including the sequence: force computer reset; set unoverlap, load mode for channel 1; select card reader and NR pocket or tape unit 0; simulate I ring 12-time for status sample; turn on channel 1 in process; 'Read end of record into storage location 0001'; then 'force program reset and auto start at 0001'. 'Only devices on channel 1 may be selected.' 'The programmer must check for correct data transfer.'
upgraded.source: A22-6726 IBM 7010 Principles of Operation, 'LOAD KEY', p. 58 - https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-6726_7010_PrincOps.pdf

upgraded.claim: J28-0249 and C20-1602-8 claims verified verbatim in their text layers: 'If the programmer requested a load program from the Autocoder Processor, he should remove the first five cards from the assembled object deck' (p. 12); 'the first five cards of the new deck MUST be discarded' (p. 26); 'the 1410 Standard Load Program (5-card loader)' (p. 35); the two Substitution Card formats storing 'N' and ',' at 00281 with the '=' glyph standing for the word separator (p. 27); and 'THE STANDARD 1410 LOAD PROGRAM... THIS IS A 9 CARD PROGRAM' with Clear Storage and Set Indexes as the last two cards, under 1410-UT-106 Individual Utility Program, distributed at the end of the UPOS program deck.
upgraded.source: J28-0249 IBM 1410 Utility Programs Part III (PAT), 1962, pp. 12, 26, 27, 35 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/J28-0249_1410_Utility_Programs_Part_III_1962.pdf ; C20-1602-8 Catalog of Programs for IBM 1410 (Jun 1968), 1410-UT-106 entry - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/C20-1602-8_1410_pgmCatJun68.pdf

upgraded.claim: The PR-108 boot line in Richard Cornwell's a.ini is exactly 'dep -c 0 1~l(b000011$~N' (fetched and hexdumped). The '~' is confirmed as SimH's word-mark prefix: i7010_sys.c parse_sym under SWMASK('C') does 'if (*cptr == '~' && wm_seen == 0) wm_seen = WM;'. ascii_to_six['('] = 034 = CHR_RPARN, which i7000_defs.h annotates '/* Also % */', so '(' is channel 1. Decoded: status char '1' at 00000; L (word-marked) at 00001; x-control '(b0' = channel 1, tape in ODD parity (binary) mode, unit 0; B-address 00011; d '$'; N (word-marked) at 00011. The record loads over the N, so after the read the IAR points at 00011, which is now the first character of the tape record.

additions.claim: The rule that explains BOTH word marks in the keyed boot string, which the findings report but never justify: 'Each instruction must have a word mark set over the operation code, and must not contain word marks in any other position. Also, a word mark must be set in the core-storage location immediately to the right of the last character of an instruction. This is normally the word mark associated with the operation code of the next sequential instruction.' The word mark on the R at 00011 is therefore not decoration or convention - it is what terminates read-out of the 10-character L instruction at 00001. Same page gives the complete set of legal instruction lengths: O = 1, Od = 2, O xxx d = 5, O aaaaa = 6, O aaaaa d = 7, O xxx bbbbb d = 10, O aaaaa bbbbb = 11, O aaaaa bbbbb d = 12.
additions.source: A22-0526-3, 'Instruction Word Marks' and 'Instruction Length Validity', p. 11 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

additions.claim: A second, simpler, and fully published 1410 CARD bootstrap that the findings missed - and the only published example of hand-keying a 1402 read on a 1410. J28-0249, 'The PAT System Tape Creation (10/20K Version)': '2. Place the card deck in the 1402 Card Reader. 3. Press READER START and END-OF-FILE. 4. Mount a scratch tape on channel 1, unit 8... 5. Clear storage from the console. 6. Display location 09247. 7. Set mode switch to ALTER and enter "L%11[0]9257%." into storage. 8. SET Instruction ADDRESS Register to location 09247. 9. Set mode switch to RUN and press START.' Word-mark carets are printed over the L and over the trailing character. Structure: the 10-character read instruction L + x-control '%11' (channel 1, card reader, stacker 1) + B-address 09257 + d occupies 09247-09256, i.e. it sits immediately below its own load address, so execution falls straight through into the card just read. No status branch is needed because this is the first I/O instruction after a reset (the interlock only stops the machine when the NEXT I/O instruction is read out). This is a strictly simpler boot shape than the Monitor's and is a better model for a hand-rolled loader. The same manual's tape twin, p. 35: 'Display location 00201. Set mode switch to ALTER and enter "L%B8[00000]$.." into storage. SET Instruction ADDRESS Register to location 00201. Set mode switch to RUN and press START.' - a read-to-end-of-core from tape unit 8 starting at 00000, which overwrites the keyed instruction itself.
additions.source: J28-0249 IBM 1410 Utility Programs Part III (PAT), 1962: card procedure on bitsavers PDF page 39 (printed p. 41, 'The PAT System Tape Creation (10/20K Version)'), a second card variant on PDF page 40, tape procedure on PDF page 34 (printed p. 35) - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/J28-0249_1410_Utility_Programs_Part_III_1962.pdf

additions.claim: The 'B' in the Monitor's tape boot string ALcBu00012$N is not a generic 'tape' selector: the x2 position of the x-control field distinguishes 'U' = magnetic tape in EVEN parity (BCD) mode from 'B' = magnetic tape in ODD parity (binary) mode. 'The odd parity mode is used for writing programs on tape.' A 1410 emulator must carry the parity mode through to the tape device, not collapse U and B. This also explains why every tape boot in the surviving literature (C28-0351-5 Tables I/II, C28-0351-5 p. 32, J28-0249 pp. 35/41, PR-108's a.ini) uses B.
additions.source: A22-0526-3, 'Read or Write Tape', p. 86 and Figure 97 footnote 'x2 = U or B (even parity or odd parity)' - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

additions.claim: Open question 6 answered for the reference emulator, and probably for the hardware: a LOAD-mode (op code L) input CLEARS pre-existing word marks in the target area, while a MOVE-mode (op code M) input PRESERVES them. SimH i7010_chan.c writes 'if ((cmd[chan] & CHAN_LOAD) == 0) ch |= M[caddr[chan]] & WM;' - the existing word mark is OR-ed back in only when NOT in load mode. This matters for the finder's question about a second boot attempt: a repeated load-mode card read into the same area does behave identically, because the previous run's word marks are wiped by the new one.
additions.source: SimH I7000/i7010_chan.c, chan_write character path - https://github.com/simh/simh/blob/master/I7000/i7010_chan.c ; consistent with A22-0526-3 'Move Mode / Load Mode', p. 41 (which describes only the word-separator conversion)

additions.claim: The 7010 'Bootstrap 1 routine card' printed alongside the 1410 one on C28-0351-5 p. 8 is a DIFFERENT card, not the same card with a different label. It reads '[word separator] R 00008 [group mark] [word separator] L x F 0 0 0 0 5 6 R [word separator] y 00025 [group mark] [word separator] L x F 1 0 0 0 5 6 $ [word separator] y 00025 2 [word separator] y 00049 [group mark] [word separator] J 00128 [word separator] a m t t t t h 2 [word separator] [group mark]' with '7010' in cols 77-80. Because the 7010 Load key loads the record at 00001 and auto-starts there, the 7010 card must carry the whole status-branch instruction itself; the 1410 card instead supplies only the I-address and d-character of the R the operator keyed at 00011. Every address on the 7010 card is exactly 10 lower than its 1410 counterpart (00008/00018, 00056/00066, 00025/00035, 00049/00059, 00128/00138).

Both C28-0351-5 initialization tables end with 'NOTE: The Asterisk-Insert switch must be set to ON.' That is a 1415 console CE switch, and A22-0526-3 explains what it does: on an odd-parity (%Bx3) tape operation a tape mark encountered mid-record produces a data check plus end-of-file, and depending on the asterisk-insert switch the tape mark character is stored as 8421-no-C, left unchanged and invalid, or converted to and stored as an asterisk. A faithful tape-boot implementation needs this switch modelled or at least stubbed to the ON behaviour.
additions.source: C28-0351-5 Tables I and II, pp. 7-8; A22-0526-3, 'Read or Write Tape with Word Marks' note, p. 87 and 'Asterisk Insert Switch' under 'IBM 1415 Console CE Test Panel' - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

additions.claim: Console ALTER has two termination rules that matter for a faithful keyed-boot implementation, and neither is in the findings: 'The alter operation continues until a word mark is sensed if one or more fields (but less than one line) were displayed. An alter operation ends when the end-of-line condition is sensed if a multi-line display preceded the alter operation.' On a freshly cleared machine there are no word marks, so the operator's ALTER of 00000-00011 runs to the end of the printer line, not to a field boundary. Also: 'If one or more fields (but less than a full line) were previously displayed, only the first displayed field can be altered.'

Further evidence bounding where the 1410 standard load program lives, which the findings do not connect: C20-1602-8's description of the 9-card standalone version says its Clear Storage card 'CLEARS ALL STORAGE ABOVE LOCATION 00499 TO BLANKS' - i.e. the load program itself must live at or below 00499. That is consistent with the standard re-entry point at 00281, with PAT keying its own tape bootstrap at 00201, and with PAT's control program occupying roughly 00000-00500.
additions.source: C20-1602-8 Catalog of Programs for IBM 1410 (Jun 1968), 1410-UT-106 entry, item 12 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/C20-1602-8_1410_pgmCatJun68.pdf ; J28-0249 pp. 12 and 35 - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/J28-0249_1410_Utility_Programs_Part_III_1962.pdf

additions.claim: The 9-card standalone 'STANDARD 1410 LOAD PROGRAM' and the Autocoder's 5-card loader are not the same deck, and the difference is accounted for: the last two of the nine are utility cards (Clear Storage, Set Indexes), leaving a 7-card loader proper versus the Autocoder's 5. Anyone reconstructing the loader should not assume the two are interchangeable.

The earliest Autocoder document, J24-1433-2 (1961), contains the EX/XFR text verbatim MINUS the sentence '(The IBM standard re-entry point is 00281.)' - the re-entry address was added in C28-0309-1. It also states a loader behaviour worth having: 'A word mark will be set in the operation code position by the loading routine at program load time.' This confirms the finder's claim that J24-1433-2 is not an earlier source for 00281.
additions.source: J24-1433-2 IBM 1410 Autocoder Preliminary Specifications, 1961, EX/XFR section and the imperative-instruction 'Result' paragraph - http://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/J24-1433-2_1410_Autocoder_Preliminary_Specifications_1961.pdf

additions.claim: Inference, not a finding: the 1410 standard load program is very likely a direct descendant of the IBM 1401 'Style 3' compiler-produced loader, and probably occupies roughly 00201-00325. The 1401 loader's segments 'ARE ASSEMBLED STARTING AT LOCATION 201' and it occupies 201-325 during execution; the 1410's published standard re-entry point 00281 falls inside that same window, PAT keys its own 1410 bootstrap at 00201, and the standalone 1410 loader clears storage only above 00499. Useful as a placement heuristic if reconstructing the deck; not documented anywhere for the 1410.
additions.source: https://ibm-1401.info/1401-CardDeckFormats.html (1401, secondary) cross-read against C28-0309-1 p. 19, J28-0249 pp. 27/35 and C20-1602-8 1410-UT-106

additions.claim: SimH's i7010 chan_boot() confirmed verbatim, and the finding's characterisation is right but understates one detail: chan_boot sets 'cmd[chan] = CHAN_NOREC|CHAN_LOAD' - i.e. the 7010 Load key is modelled as a LOAD-mode read with the group-mark-word-mark record test SUPPRESSED, reading into location 1 with IAR already 1 from reset. That NOREC flag is the same one the '$' d-character sets on a programmed read, which is the mechanical link between the 7010 Load key and the 1410's keyed 'L ... $' instruction.

notes:
Method: worked from local copies of the bitsavers PDFs plus archive.org OCR text layers, and rendered the specific figure pages at 300-400 dpi with pdftoppm where the PDFs have no text layer (C28-0351-5 p. 8, C28-0309-1 p. 7, J28-0249 pp. 34/39). SimH sources were read locally and the two files not present (i7000_sys.c does not exist; the tables are in i7010_sys.c) were located in the repo tree. a.ini was fetched and hexdumped rather than trusted from the finding.

Overall the findings are unusually accurate: the console-keying path, the 12 keyed characters, the '$'/'R'/'N' choices, the interlock mechanics, the 5-card / 9-card loader evidence and the 00281 substitution cards all survived checking against primary sources. Two claims are wrong in ways that would change emulator behaviour: the unconditional 80-character card read, and the advice to ignore the d-character on a 1402 read. Both stem from reading only the first sentence of the Read-a-Card 'Function' paragraph and stopping before the group-mark-word-mark rule.

The 1401-vs-1410 hunt turned up no 1401 facts smuggled in as 1410 facts - the findings are careful there. The conflation that IS present is 1410-vs-7010: channels 3 and 4, the '?' and '!' channel symbols and the '3' and '1' status-branch op codes are 7010-only and appear in the findings' tables without that qualification, because C28-0351-5 is a joint manual.

Untestable / still open: (a) whether real 1402 hardware sets any status indicator on a '$' read - no manual states it, and SimH's device-independent handling is evidence about the emulator, not the machine, so my correction to that claim is 'verified' for SimH and 'likely' for the hardware; (b) the exact trailing characters of J28-0249's keyed strings ('$..' and '%.') are ambiguous in the scan - the word-mark carets are printed above the line and the terminator character cannot be identified with certainty, so I quoted them literally rather than parsing them; (c) I did not run the PR-108 tape, so the finder's suggestion that the real 5-card loader can be recovered by assembling with a LOAD control card and capturing the punch file remains untested; (d) the finding 'The card images of the Autocoder 5-card loader are not published in any 1410 manual on bitsavers' is marked 'verified' but is an absence claim and cannot be verified in the strict sense - I did re-grep the text layers of C28-0309-1, J24-1433-2, C28-0326-1 (OS Autocoder), C28-0319-4 (System Monitor) and C28-0351-5 for '00281', 'load program', 'load routine' and 'five cards' and found nothing beyond what the findings already cite, so 'no counter-evidence found' is the strongest honest statement; (e) the exact printed page number of the J28-0249 card-boot procedure: the scan's page numbering has unnumbered inserts, so I cite the bitsavers PDF page (39) alongside the apparent printed page (41).
